---
title: "Quiz: grey-level morphology"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. With a flat SE $B$: erosion = min filter, dilation = max filter, opening $I \circ B$ = erode then dilate, closing $I \bullet B$ = dilate then erode; white top-hat $I - I \circ B$, black top-hat $I \bullet B - I$, gradient $(I \oplus B) - (I \ominus B)$.

---

**Q1.** A fluorescence image has small bright spots (about 5 pixels across) on a background that gets brighter towards one side. Why does a single threshold fail, and which operation fixes it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare the spot brightness on the dark side with the background brightness on the bright side.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A threshold low enough to catch the spots on the dark side is below the background on the bright side, and a threshold above the bright background misses the dim spots. A **white top-hat** with an SE larger than the spots (a disc of diameter 7–9) subtracts the opening, which follows the background but not the spots; on the top-hat the background is near 0 everywhere and one threshold works.
:::

---

**Q2.** You open a 1D profile with a flat bar of width 9. A peak is 5 samples wide at its base. What is left of it? And of a plateau 12 samples wide?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Push the bar up from below.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The bar cannot enter the 5-sample peak at any height, so the peak is cut down to the level of its surroundings: it disappears. The 12-sample plateau is wider than the bar, so the bar reaches its top: the plateau is kept at full height (only its corners can be affected if its sides are sloped).
:::

---

**Q3.** An image shows dark granules in a bright cytoplasm. Which top-hat do you use, and how do you choose the SE size?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Opening removes bright details, closing removes dark ones.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The **black top-hat** $I \bullet B - I$: the closing fills the dark granules (narrower than $B$) and follows everything else, so the difference is large exactly at the granules. $B$ must be larger than the granules and smaller than the dark structures you want to ignore (and than the scale of brightness changes in the background).
:::

---

**Q4.** What is the morphological gradient (window of 3) of the step $0\,0\,0\,0\,10\,10\,10\,10$? How does it differ from a derivative filter such as Sobel?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Max minus min in each window of 3.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$0\,0\,0\,10\,10\,0\,0\,0$: the two samples next to the step see both levels. It has no sign (a rising and a falling step look the same) and no direction, it is as large as the full step (not the slope), and it never overshoots or rings. A derivative filter gives a signed value, proportional to the slope, with a direction (horizontal or vertical Sobel).
:::

---

**Q5.** A signal has isolated bright and dark impulses ("salt and pepper"). Compare the min, the max and the median filter over a window of 3.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
A single impulse in a window of 3 is either the smallest, the largest or the middle value?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The min filter removes the bright impulses but widens every dark impulse to 3 samples; the max does the opposite. The median takes the middle value: one impulse in a window of 3 is never the middle one, so both kinds disappear, and a step between two flat levels stays sharp. All three are rank filters of the same window.
:::

---

**Q6.** Why does adding a constant brightness to the whole image not change its top-hat? Does multiplying by 2?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How do min and max behave under $I \mapsto I + c$ and $I \mapsto 2I$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\min(I + c) = \min I + c$ and $\max(I + c) = \max I + c$, so the opening shifts by $c$ too and the difference is unchanged. Multiplying by 2 (a positive factor) also commutes with min and max, so the top-hat is multiplied by 2: the same details, twice as bright. A threshold on the top-hat must therefore scale with the image contrast, but not with an offset.
:::

---

**Q7.** *(math)* Show that for a flat SE, $\{x : (I \ominus B)(x) \ge t\} = \{x : I(x) \ge t\} \ominus B$ for every threshold $t$. What does it mean for "grey-level versus binary" morphology?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
When is a minimum at least $t$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\min_{b \in B} I(x + b) \ge t \iff I(x + b) \ge t$ for all $b \in B \iff B_x \subseteq \{I \ge t\} \iff x \in \{I \ge t\} \ominus B$. So grey-level erosion (and similarly dilation, opening, closing) with a flat SE is binary morphology applied to every level set of the image, and the results stack back into a grey image. It also means: thresholding and flat morphology can be done in either order.
:::
